name: Theodemocracy
summary: Theodemocracy is Joseph Smith's 1844 idea of a government in which God holds ultimate authority and gives law, while the people consent to it and elect officers. It was meant to combine the republican forms of the US Constitution with divine rule, to protect minorities and dissent, and to prepare for the kingdom of God foretold in Daniel. It is a small, mostly historical political theology, held within the Latter Day Saint tradition and deferred to the future since the late nineteenth century.
scope: The strand of Joseph Smith, the Council of Fifty (1844-46) and Brigham Young's Utah-era use of the term, based on Smith's 1844 presidential platform, his letter using the word 'Theodemocracy', and the Council's minutes as described by the Joseph Smith Papers and Wikipedia. Most economic and social statements were never addressed by these sources and are answered at low confidence by inference; later LDS and unrelated Islamic 'theodemocracy' uses are excluded.

keyFigures.name: Joseph Smith
keyFigures.role: Coined the term Theodemocracy and organized the Council of Fifty in 1844.

keyFigures.name: Brigham Young
keyFigures.role: Carried the idea to Utah, treating republican theocracy and democratic theocracy as equivalent.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Healthcare provision was not a theodemocratic concern; the sources discuss governance and law, so the answer is a neutral inference.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The platform proposes a national bank and public land sales but no general view of markets versus government, so this is left neutral.

state-harmful.rationale: Theodemocracy holds that government is needed and ordained, to be ruled by God's law with the people's acceptance; the idea that the state is harmful is opposed to this.

empower-police-military.rationale: The platform asks that the president be able to deploy the army against mobs, though it also calls for cutting court-martials and other military punishments.

decide-locally.rationale: The system is described as loosely federal with shared sovereignty, but the platform also wants federal power to protect minorities against states.

rehabilitation.rationale: The platform urges that penitentiaries be turned into seminaries of learning and criticizes cruel imprisonment, while reserving confinement or death for murder.

more-religion-public.rationale: Theodemocracy is by definition rule by God through law with religious leaders in civic roles, so religion occupies the center of public life. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The system aims at a kingdom of God rather than a national culture; neutral.

gradual-change.rationale: The kingdom was to replace failed governments but was deferred and not forced; adherents are mixed between patient preparation and radical aim.

experts-over-public.rationale: The system holds that the people may accept or reject divinely given law, so the public keeps a voice; expert rule is not part of it.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The platform proposes a national currency and hiring freed people to labor for wages, which presumes money and wage labor.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The 1844 platform proposes a national bank with branches in every state to supply a dependable currency, the opposite of abolition.

one-party-rule.rationale: Theodemocracy had participants from beyond the church and elected leaders through republican processes; Smith ran as a candidate rather than for a single-party state.

democracy-best.rationale: Smith used vox populi vox Dei and wanted the people's consent, but held that democracy needed to be fused with divine rule; adherents are split on the 'even when voters choose badly' clause.

natural-rulers.rationale: Prophets and the Council of Fifty were held to be called by God, but the sources present this as divine appointment not natural aptitude.

political-violence-never.rationale: The movement defended itself against mobs and Smith urged using the army against them, yet the kingdom was to arrive by divine action; adherents are split.

war-builds-character.rationale: The platform calls for universal peace and for dismissing deserters rather than punishing them; war's character-building value is not claimed.

separate-church-state.rationale: Theodemocracy puts government under God's law with Church leaders in civic office, but the article says it was to be institutionally separate from the Church and Smith seemed to support separating the functions of church and state, so the opposition is qualified.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: God gives the law that the people may accept or reject, with revelation settling deadlocks; this is central, but the source is revelation more than text.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Smith held that non-members would persist in the system and be represented by non-members, and converts gathered from many nations; an ethnic nation is not the model.

class-struggle-history.rationale: History was seen as moving toward the kingdom of God foretold in Daniel, not class conflict.

civilizational-union.rationale: The kingdom was to govern the world and unite believers, so religious union is congenial, though the sources do not speak of nations uniting.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Divine law carries duties, but sources also say individual moral agency was sacred and liberties were to be protected.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental philosophy is absent from the theodemocracy sources; neutral.

restore-past-order.rationale: Restorationist theology looks back to an original church, but the kingdom is forward-looking and the sources frame it as a future order.

results-over-ideology.rationale: A system built on divine law and revelation is ideological rather than judged by results.

direct-action.rationale: The system works through republican processes, elections and councils, not direct action.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Class rule is foreign to a system of divine law with popular acceptance.

taxation-theft.rationale: The platform treats revenue and public finance as legitimate national tasks.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The system emphasizes participation and consent more than exit, though the Saints did relocate.

positive-liberty.rationale: The sources discuss liberty as protection of conscience and dissent, not as material means; neutral.

total-state.rationale: The system was not meant to be imposed on unwilling people and protected religious freedom and individual agency, which rules out totalitarian direction.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The platform argues the US is entitled to all of Oregon and welcomes Texas into the union.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on divine law and acceptance by the people, not oaths between lords and followers.

bound-labor.rationale: The platform proposes ending slavery by 1850 and hiring freed people as wage laborers.

universal-morality.rationale: God's law was to govern the world, implying universal moral truths, though they were known by revelation rather than reason.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival does not figure in theodemocracy sources.

force-without-un.rationale: The UN did not exist; the sources discuss force only domestically, so neutral.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Revelation settled deadlocks and replaced the drafted constitution in Smith's government; faith is central to the system.

workers-nation.rationale: Nothing in the sources concerns how the working class should organize.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The government was meant to serve all under divine law, not a ruling class.

national-mission.rationale: Smith held the American constitutional order inspired and that a divinely led government would eventually govern the world as the kingdom of Daniel.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about one government, party or regime, or about fighting corruption, not a general claim that most politicians put their own interests first, which this statement now asks.

reviewHistory.rationale: Council members believed existing governments had failed to protect liberty and Smith's platform proposes cutting Congress by half.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The platform has the state running a bank and a currency and carrying out moral reforms, beyond minimal government.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A question internal to Marxist debates; theodemocracy sources do not touch it.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Divine law governed the community, yet non-members were to be represented, so adherents lack a stated view.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Smith quoted Madison on avoiding interference with the rights of conscience, and the movement was missionary.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A question internal to Soviet-era socialism; no theodemocracy source addresses it.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Smith used vox populi vox Dei and the people were to accept or reject divine law, though authority rests ultimately on God.

population-transfer.rationale: The Saints were themselves expelled from Missouri and Illinois, which gives adherents reason to condemn forced removal.

separated-powers.rationale: Smith held sovereignty shared between God and the people in a loosely federal arrangement and kept civil and ecclesiastical spheres separate on paper.

vanguard-party.rationale: Class or revolutionary politics is foreign to the system.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Non-members held offices and the council included non-member participants.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Leaders were elected or divinely called, not chosen by lot.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The Saints' own persecution made them distrust majorities and governments that suspend protections.

party-controls-media.rationale: Theodemocracy is described as protecting free discussion and dissent.

party-commands-army.rationale: The platform has the president command the army; a party is not part of the model.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: The platform calls for modest per diem pay for bank officers and halving Congress, in the same spirit.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The platform would let the president use the army against mobs without waiting for a governor.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its own rationale does not support its value under the reworded statement: it describes a clerical hierarchy without bishops.

reviewHistory.rationale: The church had hierarchical offices rather than congregational governance, though bishops here are not specified.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Council of Fifty received Smith as Prophet, Priest and King, and Church leaders held civic office, though leaders were prophets, not scholars.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The kingdom was to govern the world under God's law, implying one standard.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The movement grew by gathering converts of all origins.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The system is described as protecting minority groups and conscience, and Smith appealed to rights of conscience.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Free discussion is protected but conformity to moral custom was valued.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Council drafted a constitution but Smith set it aside for revelation; adherents lacked a stated view.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Smith himself ran for president, indicating support for electing national leaders.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The platform has the national bank's profits go to national revenue rather than being independent of government.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A debate on Soviet history that the theodemocracy sources do not touch.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Theodemocracy places divine law over civil authority with church leaders in civic roles, which opposes curbing the church.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Smith's platform praised union, yet the council planned a separate theocracy elsewhere; adherents split.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Smith was received as Prophet, Priest and King, but Christ, not a mortal ruler, is the supreme king, and no divine descent is claimed.

character-from-environment.rationale: The theology stresses individual moral agency.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The ruler is bound by God's law, and the people accept or reject it; the platform calls officers servants of the people.

leader-cult.rationale: The system was not built around the leader's cult, though Smith was received as prophet and king by the council.

land-redistribution.rationale: The platform sells public lands, not seizing estates.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The movement defined community by faith rather than nationality.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Rights of conscience and religious freedom are protected, with the system not imposed on the unwilling.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The council sought a place in Texas, Oregon or California to establish a theocracy, and the Saints later left the United States for the West.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The history was seen as shaped by divine purpose toward the kingdom.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy is absent from the sources, so the answer is neutral.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Members feared the tyranny of the majority and held that constitutional protections of religious liberty were inadequate.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Offices were elected and Smith's platform treats officers as servants of the people.

public-money-creation.rationale: The platform proposes a national bank issuing currency, with profit going to national revenue, which makes money creation public.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Theodemocracy has no predecessor empire, so the question does not apply.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Council members thought existing constitutions failed to protect religious liberty and sought stronger protections.

elective-rulers.rationale: Theodemocracy elects leaders to civic offices, and Smith ran for president, though the ultimate king is Christ.

minority-veto.rationale: The Council of Fifty required full consensus and used revelation to break deadlocks.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Smith ran for president and organised a political council to prepare a kingdom of God, so withdrawal contradicts the program.

party-own-road.rationale: A question about communist parties; it does not apply to theodemocracy.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The council wanted to convert and ally with Indians, not hand them leadership.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: The platform treated slavery as a central national problem; the Civil War postdates the Council.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Theodemocracy is itself a distinct form of government meant to differ from existing ones.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The platform has the army used to protect citizens under the president, not a guardian of the constitution.

office-by-exam.rationale: Offices were filled by election or divine calling, not examination.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The platform wants officers to serve the people and Congress to be trimmed rather than abolished.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: A modern legal doctrine absent from the sources.

job-guarantee.rationale: The platform wants freed people hired to labor but gives no guarantee policy.

non-intervention.rationale: The platform urges force against mobs but is silent on foreign states.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The Saints were themselves the target of conspiracy claims, which makes adherents wary of the idea.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The council kept its records secret, but the platform's own aim is public reform.

informal-organisation.rationale: The system runs through councils and elections, not informal groups.

religious-nation.rationale: Non-members remain in a theodemocracy and are represented by non-members; the system was not to be imposed on unwilling people.

religion-illusion.rationale: Theodemocracy is defined by divine rule and revelation, so religion is true and basic.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Historical judgments on capitalism are absent from theodemocracy sources.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Dissent and free discussion are described as protected in a theodemocracy.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Smith appealed to rights of conscience and Wikipedia says the system was not meant for the unwilling.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Smith's circle expected existing governments to fall to divine action rather than armed overthrow; adherents split.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Intersectionality is a modern framework absent from the sources.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Wikipedia says God holds ultimate authority and gives law that the people may accept or reject, which is the defining claim of theodemocracy.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The platform relies on the army to protect citizens against mobs.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Christ is the supreme king and mortal leaders are called or elected, not inherited.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The platform proposes a national bank but not a mutual one.

property-franchise.rationale: Elections included members of the community and non-members, with no property test stated.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The sources discuss free discussion but not who owns the presses.

racial-franchise.rationale: Participation was by community consent and included non-members; racial tests are not part of the system.

open-government-data.rationale: The council met in confidence, but the platform treats officers as servants of the people.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Mormons were themselves boycotted and attacked as a minority.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Continuing revelation allows change, yet adherents did not frame it as reinterpretation.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The system is built around God, so it cannot promote atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about prisons or punishment, and the statement now asks only whether the police should be abolished.

reviewHistory.rationale: The platform reforms prisons and keeps confinement for murder rather than abolishing them.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about prisons or punishment, and the statement now asks only whether the police should be abolished.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The Council required full consensus and protection of minorities.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Smith's circle held both consecration of property and private ownership; the sources do not settle it.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Theodemocracy places God's authority over government and looks to the kingdom of God of Daniel's prophecy, framing politics as part of a divine order against worldly rule.

person-over-state.rationale: Smith's platform and the Council of Fifty aimed to protect minorities and dissenters from majority and mob power, giving individuals rights the community may not override.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Theodemocracy rests on God holding ultimate authority and giving law, so politics is meant to serve spiritual as well as civic ends.

arms-reduction.rationale: Smith's platform proposed reducing the army's role in some respects but also federal force to protect minorities, so no clear stance on armaments follows.

open-diplomacy.rationale: The Council of Fifty met in secret, yet the platform did not address treaties; no clear position follows.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Smith's platform wanted debts paid from land sales, but no legal borrowing limit is stated; neutral inference.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The sources give no economic blueprint; the Council of Fifty debated governance rather than economic systems.

sacred-nation.rationale: Smith held the Constitution divinely inspired and looked to a covenant kingdom, so a sacred community is plausible, though it is the kingdom, not the nation, that is central.

farm-price-support.rationale: Agricultural policy was not a theodemocratic concern; the sources discuss governance and law.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Property rights of women were not treated in the sources, and nineteenth-century practice varied.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Smith's theodemocracy was meant to protect the rights and dissent of all faiths and minorities, though it also expects God's law to hold final authority.

indirect-election.rationale: Smith's platform favoured popular consent and elected officers while the Council of Fifty was appointed, so the sources point both ways.

missingStatements.text: Government should combine laws revealed by God with the consent of the people.
missingStatements.rationale: Smith's theodemocracy has God give the law and the people accept or reject it, with vox populi vox Dei.

missingStatements.text: The national government should be able to send the army to protect a religious minority from mobs without waiting for a state governor's request.
missingStatements.rationale: Smith's 1844 platform proposed this after the Missouri persecutions.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to 1844 American context and not answerable by most ideologies.

missingStatements.text: Slavery should be ended gradually, with slaveholders compensated from the sale of public lands.
missingStatements.rationale: Smith's platform proposed ending slavery by 1850 with compensation from federal land sales.
missingStatements.declined: Specific historical policy of the 1844 platform; not a general position.

notes: Sources on theodemocracy address governance, religious liberty and a few 1844 policy proposals; most economic and social answers are low-confidence inferences, so inclusion may be thin. Whether Smith meant to establish it before the Second Coming is unclear.
